articles.title: Britain's seagrass meadows were disappearing; a Scottish community transplanted mature shoots instead of seeds and achieved 97% survival
articles.summary: UK News: Britain's seagrass meadows have suffered decades of decline, but a community-led project on Scotland's west coast is showing that restoring them may n.
articles.body: Britain's seagrass meadows have suffered decades of decline, but a community-led project on Scotland's west coast is showing that restoring them may not always require starting from seeds. Seawilding, a Scottish marine restoration charity, has been experimenting with transplanting mature Zostera marina shoots from healthy donor meadows into areas where seagrass has been lost. The approach has produced striking early results at Loch Craignish in Argyll, including a 97% survival rate in a 2025 trial. In another restoration plot, seabed coverage increased from 10% to more than 70% within 15 months. Together, the trials have created about 0.3 hectares of new seagrass habitat, offering a promising alternative for restoring an ecosystem that supports marine life, stabilises sediments and stores carbon.Scotland's disappearing seagrass gets a new restoration approachSeagrasses are flowering marine plants that form underwater meadows in shallow coastal waters. Scotland has two native species, Zostera marina and Zostera noltii, with Z. marina, commonly known as eelgrass, occurring widely along the country's coastline. These habitats provide nursery and feeding areas for marine organisms, help stabilise sediments and contribute to coastal protection and blue-carbon storage. Yet seagrass beds are vulnerable to physical disturbance, poor water quality, disease and other pressures. NatureScot notes that modelled estimates for Britain indicate a general decline of at least 44% in seagrass beds, although it also cautions that historical and Scottish data are incomplete and that the extent of change is difficult to establish precisely.Seawilding began its community-led restoration work in Loch Craignish, Argyll, with earlier efforts concentrating on collecting and planting seagrass seeds. The organisation says that, over roughly a decade, UK restoration efforts have focused largely on seed-based approaches, but establishing large areas of new meadow has often proved difficult. From 2024, Seawilding began testing a different strategy by taking adult shoots from existing healthy meadows and transplanting them into suitable restoration sites.Instead of waiting for seeds, the team moved mature plantsThe key difference in Seawilding's newer approach is that the restoration team starts with living adult seagrass shoots rather than relying entirely on seeds to germinate and establish new plants. Tens of thousands of shoots have been transplanted from donor meadows into restoration areas at Loch Craignish. The idea is relatively straightforward: establish living plants immediately in suitable seabed rather than waiting for seeds to germinate, survive their early development and eventually develop into mature plants.The technique is not entirely unprecedented. NatureScot's Scottish seagrass restoration guidance notes that transplantation has been used elsewhere and can offer advantages where restoration needs to overcome physical problems that make establishment from seed difficult. However, transplantation can also require considerably more labour because plants have to be collected and replanted. The Scottish guidance therefore stresses that restoration success depends on choosing an appropriate technique for the environmental conditions rather than assuming one method will work everywhere.Seawilding's project also grew out of several years of experimentation. The organisation says it trialled multiple restoration methods before the adult-shoot approach began producing the results reported in 2025. That history is important because the 97% figure did not come from a single attempt that immediately succeeded. It followed repeated trials to determine how best to collect, transport and establish the plants.A 2025 trial recorded 97% survivalThe strongest result came from a new transplantation trial conducted in 2025. Seawilding reported that 97% of the transplanted shoots survived, while the trial area also recorded an average fourfold increase in seabed coverage within six months. This result is separate from another restoration plot where coverage increased from 10% to more than 70% over 15 months. Taken together, the results indicate that transplanted adult plants can establish rapidly under the conditions tested at Loch Craignish.The longer-running plot began receiving transplanted shoots in July 2024. By the following 15 months, the proportion of seabed covered by seagrass had risen from 10% to more than 70%. Across the reported restoration work, Seawilding says the intervention has resulted in approximately 0.3 hectares of newly created seagrass habitat. The organisation describes the results as among the most successful establishments of seagrass habitat in the UK to date, although those claims should be understood as project-level results rather than evidence that Britain's seagrass decline has been reversed.The project also investigated what happened to the original donor meadow after shoots were removed. Seawilding reports that harvesting 25% of shoots from a trial area had a limited apparent effect, with shoot density returning to near-natural levels within about five months. This is particularly important because a restoration technique would be difficult to scale if collecting plants simply damaged existing healthy meadows.Local people are helping rebuild the underwater habitatThe Scottish project is notable not only for its restoration technique but also for its community-led structure. Seawilding describes itself as Scotland's first community-based marine habitat restoration charity, and local volunteers have been involved in monitoring, planting and other stages of the work. The organisation's earlier Loch Craignish project was developed with technical support from Project Seagrass and research and environmental monitoring from the Scottish Association of Marine Sciences.Community participation has also been important for understanding the condition of the existing meadows before restoration begins. NatureScot's case study describes local residents surveying Loch Craignish using transects and quadrats to record seagrass coverage, while snorkellers and paddleboarders have helped with field observations and seed collection. The earlier project also held public restoration events where residents could learn about seagrass and participate in collection and planting activities.This community involvement fits a wider body of research showing that restoration projects can benefit when local communities are involved in designing and delivering conservation rather than being treated simply as observers. A 2025 peer-reviewed study of a major UK seagrass restoration project in Wales found that changing the approach towards co-production helped rebuild trust between the restoration team and local stakeholders. The study also found that the restored site had begun showing positive ecological development, although large-scale continuous meadow recovery remained incomplete.The results are promising but the method still needs wider testingThe Loch Craignish results are encouraging, but they do not yet establish that transplanting mature shoots will work everywhere in Britain. Seagrass survival depends on factors including depth, sediment, exposure, water movement, light and local ecological conditions. NatureScot also identifies significant knowledge gaps around Scottish seagrass, including habitat suitability, connectivity, disease and the ecosystem benefits of restoration.Seawilding is now taking the next step by testing the technique at additional locations along Scotland's west coast. Supported by the Blue Carbon Trust, trials are planned at Ganavan Bay near Oban, Loch na Cille and Port na Carraigh on the Isle of Gigha. Each site is intended to test how transplanted shoots perform under different environmental conditions and whether using locally sourced plants produces different results from shoots originating at Loch Craignish. Monitoring is planned through 2027.The significance of the project therefore lies less in the claim that one Scottish community has solved seagrass restoration and more in the evidence that a relatively simple change in strategy can produce striking early results. Rather than waiting for seeds to establish naturally, the team is moving mature plants into suitable habitat and monitoring whether they survive and expand. If the approach continues to work at different sites without damaging donor meadows, it could become another practical tool for restoring Britain's fragmented underwater meadows.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Game on, history off: White House unveils MAGA arcade
articles.summary: US News: TOI correspondant from Washington: America has spent 250 years arguing about how it was built. The White House has now settled the matter in the most .
articles.body: TOI correspondant from Washington: America has spent 250 years arguing about how it was built. The White House has now settled the matter in the most authoritative medium available to the United States: a video game.The Trump administration on Friday unveiled “Arcade,” five retro-style games on the official White House website, turning pieces of President Trump’s MAGA agenda into pixelated entertainment. The collection includes games titled “Build the Wall,” “Rio Run,” “Supply Line,” “Flappy Bill” and “Trump Savings Tycoon.”If this sounds like something dreamed up by a teenager who has consumed too much caffeine, that is roughly the aesthetic. The White House promotional material riffs on the loading screens of Xbox, PlayStation and Nintendo, even transforming the Sega logo into “MAGA.” The launch slogan was suitably subtle: “Can’t stop winning. Build the wall. Deport. Fill a Trump Account.”But two immigration games are generating fireworks. “Build the Wall” is essentially Tetris, a Soviet-era game, with immigration policy overtones.Players stack wall sections to “protect the border from the coming hordes.”“Rio Run,” modeled on the game Snake, puts a digital character resembling border czar Tom Homan on patrol along the Rio Grande, where the object is to collect illegal aliens. Captured characters trail behind in orange prison uniforms -- in other words, ICE meets Pac-Man.Immigration-rights advocates have reacted with fury, saying the games turn human beings and matters involving detention, family separation, deportation, asylum claims -- life-or-death issues for some — into entertainment. The criticism has also extended to the use of government resources, with the White House accused of misusing taxpayer money to produce political propaganda and of dehumanizing migrants.Trump supporters naturally see it differently, arguing that the administration is simply communicating policy in a language younger Americans understand.The White House says it is “laser focused” on innovative ways of telling the story of Trump's accomplishments and contrasting its “culture of fun and winning” with what it calls the Democrats' “dark socialist vision.”But critics say there is a larger MAGA project lurking beneath the pixels: the rewriting — or, supporters would say, correcting — of America's historical narrative.The MAGA folks have spent years pushing a more patriotic interpretation of the American story. Trump's 1776 Commission was explicitly created to promote “patriotic education,” – aka known among critics as “whitewashed history” – which the current administration revived in 2025.This year's official 250th-anniversary rhetoric celebrates the Founders, liberty and America's exceptionalism, emphasizing the nation's triumphs rather than dwelling on its darker chapters.Such an approach collides with the tradition represented by the historian Howard Zinn, whose A People's History of the United States deliberately shifted attention toward people left out of the conventional triumphal story -- Native Americans, enslaved people, workers, immigrants and the poor.Zinn's critics regard that account as excessively one-sided; his admirers regard it as a necessary antidote to sanitized history.The uncomfortable historical footnote is that America's story was never simply Europeans arriving, building, and prospering. Long before Ellis Island opened in 1892, the US already contained immigrants who never saw that gateway. African Americans, overwhelmingly descended from people brought forcibly to America during slavery, were moving from the South toward Northern cities in significant numbers beginning in the 1890s.And on the opposite coast, the first recorded Sikh arrivals in California came in 1899, before the great Ellis Island wave had run its course.Meanwhile, the people who were already here — Native Americans, also wrongly called Indians — disappear altogether from the arcade version of MAGA's immigration and national origin story.In the White House’s new version of America, history has been simplified, immigration has been gamified, and the uncomfortable parts have apparently been left on the cutting-room floor.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Lindsay Clancy judge says he’ll declare a mistrial, but grants defense one hour to appeal
articles.summary: A Massachusetts judge said he would declare a mistrial Friday after the jury weighing the fate of Lindsay Clancy failed for the third time to reach a verdict in the case of the mother accused of the strangling deaths of her three young children in 2023.
articles.body: A Massachusetts judge said he would declare a mistrial Friday after the jury weighing the fate of Lindsay Clancy failed for the third time to reach a verdict in the case of the mother accused of the strangling deaths of her three young children in 2023. But in a dramatic courtroom moment, Clancy’s lawyer said he wanted to appeal to a higher court. The judge granted him one hour to do so. Judge William Sullivan made the announcement after the jury sent the court a note saying it was still deadlocked. “I’m going to declare a mistrial at this point,” Sullivan told the court Friday morning. Both the prosecution and defense were given the opportunity to opine on the decision after the third deadlock. Defense attorney Kevin Reddington fought hard against a mistrial, asking for a final emergency appeal to the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts, but Sullivan seemed against bringing the jury back Saturday to continue deliberating should Reddington win the appeal. Sullivan told Reddington he had one hour to file an emergency stay before calling the jurors back to dismiss them. But Reddington has a “very low probability” of winning that appeal, said Danny Cevallos, NBC News legal analyst. Although it’s Reddington’s job to try “absolutely everything” to avoid a mistrial, Cevallos said the defense isn’t likely to get the interim relief that they are seeking. Clancy had pleaded not guilty to three first-degree murder charges in the deaths of Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months. But the jury remained deadlocked after a nearly six-week trial and seven days of deliberation. The jury was tasked with determining whether Clancy was criminally responsible in her children’s deaths, or whether she was not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility because of mental illness. Sullivan got the first deadlock note Tuesday, the fourth day of deliberations, and dismissed the jurors after asking them to continue to work toward a verdict. On Wednesday, the jury issued a second note saying it is “still unable to come to a unanimous decision.” Sullivan, at that point, read the jurors what’s known as Tuey-Rodriguez instructions, which essentially asks them to give deliberations one last chance and tells them that it’s “desirable” they reach a verdict. Under Massachusetts law, a judge can only ask a jury to keep deliberating twice, unless it consents to further deliberations. If the jury still cannot reach a unanimous verdict after the third deadlock, the judge can declare a mistrial, which Sullivan did. Clancy’s defense argued she was not criminally responsible for the Jan. 24, 2023, killings because she was mentally ill with postpartum psychosis, a rare condition that can alter a new mother’s sense of reality and is considered a psychiatric emergency. It is more severe and less common than postpartum depression. Her attorneys argued that she had mentally deteriorated over the preceding months and, despite repeated efforts to seek psychiatric help including calling the suicide hotline, she was never properly diagnosed. Instead, she was given a spate of different medications over a matter of months to treat her symptoms or the adverse reactions to some of the medications. In closing arguments, Reddington blamed “the damn medicine and the lousy medical care that she got” for the trajectory from happy family to the murders. He claimed the prosecution was trying to manipulate the jury by portraying Clancy as control-obsessed and for downplaying the severity of her suicide attempt, which left her paralyzed from the waist down. He doubled down on Clancy’s claim that she heard a male voice compelling her to kill her kids — a point the prosecution has tried to pick apart in trial. She told a hospital chaplain about the voice, and told her then-husband over the phone in a call heard by a forensic psychologist. He also emphasized the testimony of forensic psychiatrist Dr. Phillip Resnick who concluded that Clancy was psychotic at the time of the murders. “This young lady is not guilty of the killing of her children because she was suffering from a disease and defect,” Reddington said. Prosecutors argued Clancy was in full control of her faculties at the time of the killings and deliberately planned the murders. They acknowledged that she was struggling with her mental health, but claimed she manipulated her doctors and treatment and argued that she was not in psychosis at the time of the killings. They argued she intentionally sent her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, out to pick up dinner and go to CVS the evening of the murders. They said she looked up how long the trip would take and called the store to make sure it had a medication in stock to buy herself enough time. Then, Clancy methodically killed the kids one after another and then attempted suicide by throwing herself out of her second-story bedroom window, prosecutors said. Patrick Clancy testified that he returned home that evening to find “blood everywhere.” Clancy was bleeding on the ground outside their home, he said. The children were in the basement, unresponsive and with exercise bands around their necks. While the trial has seen Clancy emerge as a symbol of the problems plaguing maternal healthcare, in her closing arguments, Plymouth County Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague told the jury this trial wasn’t about the mental health system or how it treats women. Sprague conceded Clancy had mental health issues and was depressed. But, she said, it wasn’t the fault of the providers that Clancy wasn’t getting better. In the months leading up to the killings, Clancy told family members she was getting better but told psychiatrist, Dr. Jennifer Tufts, that she was depressed, Sprague said. But she didn’t tell Tufts the whole story either, Sprague said. During her sessions with Tufts, Clancy “denied having a suicide plan, denied wanting to hurt anyone else, denied voices” and “showed no signs of psychosis.” Sprague walked the jury through the killings, detailing how Clancy used the exercise bands to strangle her children, calling it as “extreme atrocity and cruelty.” “Those kids were her protective factor,” Sprague said. “Those kids were keeping her from ending her misery. And so she had to remove the protective factor. … It was a choice.” The livestreamed trial captivated the nation and prompted an outcry of support for Clancy, with hundreds gathering outside of the courtroom in solidarity. It also spawned conspiracy theories and chatter on social media by armchair crime junkies. For additional resources, visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources.

articles.title: Safety manager accused of killing 5-year-old boy in hyperbaric oxygen chamber fire sentenced to prison
articles.summary: A man has been sentenced to more than a year in prison in connection with the death of a boy who was killed in a fiery explosion inside a hyperbaric oxygen chamber last year.
articles.body: A man has been sentenced to more than a year in prison in connection with the death of a boy who was killed in a fiery explosion inside a hyperbaric oxygen chamber last year. Jeffrey Mosteller, 66, pleaded no contest to involuntary manslaughter in Oakland County circuit court in Michigan on Monday in connection with the death of 5-year-old Thomas Cooper. Mosteller will serve 19 months in prison, avoiding the maximum penalty of 15 years behind bars. He was the safety manager at the Oxford Center, an alternative health care center that treats children with various health conditions — including autism, ADHD, and autoimmune diseases — through hyperbaric oxygen therapy. Cooper, of Detroit suburb Royal Oak, died while undergoing treatment at the center in January 2025 after the hyperbaric chamber caught fire from the inside and exploded. His family’s attorney, James Harrington, previously told NBC News that the boy was going to the Oxford Center to treat sleep apnea and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Harrington also told NBC News that the boy’s mother rushed toward the chamber when the fire ignited, burning her arm in an unsuccessful attempt to save her son. The boy was burned alive in front of her, the lawyer said, Prosecutors have accused the center of “deliberately disregarding” safety protocols set by both the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) and Sechrist Industries, the manufacturer of the hyperbaric chamber. Mosteller was one of four former Oxford Center employees criminally charged in connection with the boy’s death. Tamela Peterson, the clinic’s owner, and Gary Marken, the facility’s primary management assistant, each face a single charge of second-degree murder or involuntary manslaughter. Aleta Moffitt, the operator of the hyperbaric chamber, was charged with one count of falsifying medical records for allegedly entering false information on a patient chart. The three other former employees have pleaded not guilty and are awaiting trial. Mosteller could face additional prison time and be denied parole after 19 months if he behaves poorly behind bars. “I expect his conduct will be stellar and I hope that he will be released at the 19-month mark,” his attorney, Alona Sharon, said in a statement. The Michigan Attorney General’s Office did not immediately return a request for comment. In July, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced that a plea agreement had been reached with Mosteller. “A young child lost his life in a completely preventable tragedy because this defendant allowed an outdated device to operate in defiance of safety standards,” Nessel said in a statement at the time. “While no outcome can reverse this loss, it is my hope that this conviction provides a sense of justice to Thomas’s family.” Cooper’s parents filed a civil lawsuit against the Oxford Center and Sechrist, seeking $100 million in damages over the boy’s death.

articles.title: UN raises ‘ethnic cleansing’ concerns over Israeli West Bank operation
articles.summary: More than 33,000 Palestinian refugees remain displaced since Israel launched Operation Iron Wall.
articles.body:
A United Nations report found that Israel's military actions in the West Bank have led to the displacement of thousands of Palestinians, raising concerns of ethnic cleansing.

Operation Iron Wall conducted by Israel resulted in the killing of 102 Palestinians and the displacement of over 33,000 residents from three refugee camps.

The UN report concluded that Israel's actions may constitute a crime against humanity of forcible transfer, as the military operation aimed to expel Palestinians and make way for illegal Israeli settlements.

Israel's military actions resulting in the displacement of entire Palestinian populations in three refugee camps in the occupied West Bank "appear to amount to collective punishment and raise concerns of ethnic cleansing", a United Nations Human Rights report has found.

Israel's Operation Iron Wall in January and February 2025 killed 102 Palestinians and displaced more than 33,000 residents from the Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem refugee camps, said the report, titled Destruction of Palestinian refugee camps in northern West Bank.

Displaced Palestinians reported being told by Israeli officers that there would be no more refugee camps and that they should "all go to Jordan".

Such large-scale, long-term and systematic displacement of the Palestinian population could amount to a crime against humanity of forcible transfer, the report by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said on Friday.

It stressed that the use of air strikes, armoured bulldozers and controlled detonations to render entire areas uninhabitable and prevent the return of residents, in the absence of imperative military necessity, is not permissible under international law.

"The way Operation Iron Wall has been conducted suggests its aim was to expel as many Palestinians as possible and to make way for more illegal Israeli settlements, in further violation of international law," said UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk.

The three camps are among a total of 19 in the West Bank that were established to shelter Palestinian refugees after the mass forced expulsion during the Nakba in 1948 and have been administered by the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA).

As of July, about 33,362 displaced Palestinian refugees from these camps remained forcibly displaced, according to UNRWA.

At least 21 children were killed by Israeli forces during the military operation in the period covered by the report. Saddam Hussein Rajab, aged 10, was shot in the stomach in Tulkarem while waiting for his father to go to the mosque. In Jenin, a two-year-old girl was shot in the head by Israeli forces while having dinner with her mother and aunt.

The report stressed that Israel "must end its unlawful presence in the occupied Palestinian territory as rapidly as possible" and "halt any efforts to forcibly displace more Palestinians".

articles.title: At least 37 killed by toxic fumes during alleged petrol theft in Nigeria, reports say
articles.summary: An environmental group says those who died are suspected of stealing petrol from a pipeline in Nigeria's Rivers State.
articles.body:
At least 37 people have died after inhaling toxic fumes while allegedly stealing petrol from a pipeline in Nigeria's Rivers State, an environmental group in the oil-rich region says.

Many are still missing after more than 100 people descended on Okari Jetty in Okrika in small boats to collect the refined fuel under cover of darkness, according to the Youths and Environmental Advocacy Centre (YEAC).

The police told the BBC an investigation was ongoing to determine the figures of those affected after people reportedly collapsed - with local reports saying some fell into the Bonny River while others were taken to hospital.

Theft from pipelines has been a problem for decades in Nigeria's oil hub.

Rivers is one of several states that make up the southern Niger Delta region, a vast area of swamps and wetlands with huge reserves of oil and gas along Nigeria's coast.

For years, criminal groups have tapped pipelines and siphon crude oil or other petroleum products into boats and storage tanks, to be sold on the black market or taken to illegal refineries.

Shell pumped oil through Nigeria pipeline for years despite pollution evidence, documents show

The YEAC said its network of volunteers and human rights defenders had reported that people in Okrika had died after inhaling what it locally known as "Indorama fuel", which is a form of refined petrol known as PMS (Premium Motor Spirit).

Nigeria's Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) has urged the public and media to rely on verified information as they work with other security agencies to establish what happened in the early hours of Thursday morning.

It condemned illegal tapping and siphoning, warning that such activities put lives, the environment and the economy at risk.

Similarly, many campaigners have also blamed the practice for contributing to environmental damage.

The government has stepped up operations against oil theft in recent years.

On Thursday, the director of navel information, Capt Abiodun Folorunsho, warned thieves there was "no hiding place" from the navy, which patrols the waterways and coastal areas of the Niger Delta.

"Their days are numbered, and if we catch you, of course, we'll ensure that you face the law," he said in an interview with Nigerian broadcaster Channels TV.

While the Nigerian navy has increased maritime security operations, the military and other security agencies have carried out operations against oil thieves, who often hid out in the area's dense mangrove forests.

Nigeria is trying to increase oil production after years of problems caused by theft, insecurity and underinvestment.

The country aims to raise production to about three million barrels per day by 2030 and is relying on better security and reforms to attract new investment.

articles.summary: UK News: The luxury mansion belonging to late boxing legend Ricky Hatton has finally been sold for £1.5 million, £350,000 below its original asking price, acco.
articles.body: The luxury mansion belonging to late boxing legend Ricky Hatton has finally been sold for £1.5 million, £350,000 below its original asking price, according to Land Registry documents cited by the Daily Mail.The five-bedroom detached property in Gee Cross, Greater Manchester, was initially listed for £1.85 million. However, following Hatton’s death last September, the home was taken off the market before being relisted at a series of reduced prices. It was eventually sold earlier this year for £1.5 million.Mansion was taken off market after Ricky Hatton’s deathHatton, a former light-welterweight and welterweight world champion, was found dead at the property in September 2025, aged 46. His body was discovered in the games room by his manager Paul Speak.The house had reportedly been placed on the market for £1.85 million shortly before his death. Following the tragedy, the sale was paused before the property returned to the market at £1.75 million. The asking price was subsequently reduced to £1.65 million before the eventual £1.5 million sale.Despite the circumstances surrounding the property, the estate agent’s listing made no reference to Hatton’s death. Instead, it described the residence as a “landmark modern residence offering luxury, space and unrivalled lifestyle features”.Inside Ricky Hatton’s lavish homeBuilt in 2010, the six-bathroom property had been extensively personalised by Hatton and reflected several of his passions, particularly his love for Manchester City.The grounds reportedly featured a traditional telephone box as well as seats from the club’s former Maine Road stadium. The property also offered expansive landscaped gardens with views of the surrounding greenbelt.Among its luxury amenities were a heated indoor swimming pool and jacuzzi, a private gym, cinema room and games room with a bar. A glass wall in the games area overlooked the pool.The principal bedroom suite featured a dressing room or walk-in closet, a deluxe en-suite bathroom, a crushed velvet chaise longue and dark patterned wallpaper.The mansion also included multiple reception rooms, open-plan living areas and a high-specification dark-panelled kitchen. CCTV and intercom access provided additional security.The estate agent described it as a “rare opportunity to acquire a truly outstanding home” in one of the North West’s most sought-after residential areas.Sale comes amid questions over Ricky Hatton’s estateThe property sale comes amid reports of uncertainty surrounding Hatton’s wider fortune. In July, reports claimed that disagreements had emerged over his estimated £40 million estate, with some members of his close family reportedly unclear about how his wealth would ultimately be distributed.Hatton, widely known by his nickname “The Hitman”, retired from boxing in 2012 after a celebrated career that saw him become a two-weight world champion and one of Britain’s most recognisable fighters.His death at the age of 46 sent shockwaves through the boxing world, with tributes pouring in from fighters, trainers and fans around the globe.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: La jefa de Gabinete de SailGP hace balance de estas seis temporadas de competición, de su crecimiento y desgrana los planes de futuro de la liga de catamaranes voladores
articles.body: Alejandra Mato, jefa de Gabinete de SailGP y mano derecha de Russell Coutts, CEO de la liga de catamaranes voladores que superan los 100 km/h, destila pasión al hablar de la vela, la competición y del Gran Premio de España en Valencia por primera vez. "Por fin ha llegado el momento de estar aquí, teníamos muchas ganas", dice con una amplia sonrisa. La directiva española guarda un gran recuerdo de los cuatro últimos años en los que se celebró en Cádiz. "Allí nos han tratado fenomenal siempre y el público ha sido espectacular, pero teníamos que crecer y era necesario llegar a una gran ciudad", explica la madrileña, aunque se mudó hace 23 años a la capital del Turia. El acuerdo con la Comunidad Valenciana es, en principio, por tres años. "Hemos montado un estadio, que es nuestro ADN, justo mirando a la Malvarrosa. Van a ver súper cerca a los barcos, te pasan por delante y casi te mojan. Queremos que nos sigan a quienes les guste el motor y la velocidad. No somos un evento de vela, somos un evento de entretenimiento”, explica. Por eso la Fórmula 1 del mar emplea palabras más cercanas a la F1 que a la vela "para que todo el mundo pueda entenderlo". No hablan de nudos sino de km/h, tampoco de regatas sino de carreras, el patrón es el piloto y la vela es el ala, porque es rígida y se asemeja al ala de un avión. "Lo que hacemos es abrir la vela a todo el mundo y democratizar el deporte. Las carreras duran 15 minutos y son en un formato que permite un espectáculo completamente diferente", asegura. Mato argumenta el concepto de entretenimiento, no sólo en las retransmisiones. "La gente viene con sus familias, tenemos food trucks, un simulador, tiramos camisetas a las gradas y tenemos un DJ y pantallas gigantes con comentarista en directo. Es todo un espectáculo destinado a disfrutar", asegura. En la primera temporada de SailGP, en 2019, la flota la componían ocho barcos que representaban a ocho naciones. Hoy son 13 países con sus 13 F50 iguales y que compiten en 13 ciudades a lo largo de la temporada. Y entre los inversores hay nombres tan destacados como Mbappé en el equipo francés, Sebastian Vettel en el alemán o los actores Ryan Reynolds y Hugh Jackman en el australiano o Anne Hathaway, en el italiano. La temporada siguiente habrá, como mínimo, 14 equipos y la idea es seguir creciendo y llegar a 24 eventos en un futuro y 20 equipos. "Pero tenemos que ir creciendo con cabeza. Tenemos un plan de estrategia porque en el 2030 queremos estar entre los 25 eventos deportivos más importantes a nivel mundial", dice. Y echando la vista atrás, a los inicios de SailGP en 2019, sonríe. "Ni de lejos me imaginaba llegar a este punto en seis temporadas. El 68% de la gente que experimenta SailGP viene a más de un evento. Lo que demuestra es que el producto funciona y que la gente tiene interés. Yo todos los días me pellizco y digo, esto no puede ser verdad", dice orgullosa. Igual de orgullosa que al hablar de 'Los Gallos', el equipo español, que este año llevan siete podios en los siete Grandes Premios que han navegado. "Son un equipazo brutal y tienen un potencial impresionante. Son una amenaza real para todos los equipos de SailGP. Se me ponen los pelos de punta porque es impresionante", dice a la vez que señala la carne de gallina que se le ha puesto.

articles.title: Russian drone hits Ukranian security headquarters, Zelensky says
articles.summary: The unmanned aerial vehicle struck without warning in the heart of the Ukrainian capital.
articles.body:
A Russian drone has hit the headquarters of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) during a strike in the heart of Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

The unmanned aerial vehicle crashed into the SBU headquarters on Friday afternoon, targeting a room used by security chief Oleksandr Poklad.

It is not clear whether Poklad was in the building, but Zelensky said he had since spoken to him to order an "appropriate, tangible response".

"The drone was aimed directly at the office of the Head of the Security Service in that building," Zelensky confirmed. It suggests Russia's new drones are growing in accuracy and signals Moscow could step up strikes before possible US mediation talks this weekend.

Trump's peace envoys to visit Moscow and Kyiv over weekend, reports say

"All emergency services are on the scene. Everyone affected will receive the necessary assistance," Zelensky added in a message on Telegram.

"I instructed Poklad to deliver an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike, to the Russians once everything is ready. Our military will support this response."

Images of the office widely shared online showed black smoke pouring from two windows on the front of the building.

Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said the attack was a "major escalation that demands resolute responses".

"Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace - laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy," he added.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people had been hurt in the SBU attack, but did not elaborate on whether they were inside the offices.

A nearby café was damaged and one customer was taken to hospital after the strike.

Stanislav Zavertaylo, co-owner of the popular Zavertailo chain, told the BBC that this was his third café to have been damaged since the start of the full-scale invasion.

"Now I'm in shock because there's a lot of damage. All the windows are broken, there's a lot of glass, garbage" he added.

The Russian defence ministry also said on Friday it had struck a cargo vessel in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk and a tanker near Odesa.

In recent weeks Russia has escalated its daytime strikes on Ukrainian targets.

In many instances it has employed jet-powered drones which are faster and harder to intercept. It is not yet known which type of munition was used in this latest attack.

The strike on the SBU building is a rare example of Russia successfully hitting a government building.

Previously Ukrainian offices have remained unscathed despite attempts from the Kremlin to stifle defences to its advances.

The SBU - which is just over the road from the St Sophia cathedral, the oldest building in Kyiv - is a key part of Ukraine's war efforts as it conducts deep strikes to damage Russian infrastructure.

The drone came during yet another air raid alert. There was a brief whine before an explosion echoed across the roof tops and smoke rose into the sky.

Despite the ongoing exchanges, US mediators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Russia and Ukraine this weekend, reports say, as efforts to end the war continue.

The envoys will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday in Moscow, and then will hold talks with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday in Kyiv, Axios said, citing US officials.

Witkoff and Kushner have led US President Donald Trump's efforts to broker a peace deal, without a breakthrough so far.

articles.title: Three hurricanes churn in the Pacific, one that could affect Hawaii, as El Niño ramps up
articles.summary: Three hurricanes — Karina, Lowell and Marie — are churning in the Pacific Ocean, a high level of activity that climate scientists say is on brand for El Niño.
articles.body: Three hurricanes — Karina, Lowell and Marie — are churning in the Pacific Ocean, a high level of activity that climate scientists say is on brand for El Niño, especially given that this year’s event is likely to become the strongest on record. Two of the storms hit major hurricane status this week. Lowell, which could target Hawaii this weekend, reached Category 5 strength Wednesday and has since weakened to Category 3. The storm is moving west but expected to make a sharp turn to the north over the weekend, according to the National Hurricane Center, taking it near the islands of Oahu and Kauai. The forecast comes as Hawaii is still recovering from multiple instances of heavy rain and flash flooding over the last six months. Just weeks ago, parts of Oahu and the Big Island were hit with intense flooding and strong winds from Tropical Storm Lala. Damage also remains from devastating floods in March, when more than 25 inches of rain fell in some parts of Oahu and more than 19 inches in parts of Maui. Meanwhile, Karina has weakened from Category 3 to Category 2 east of the Hawaiian islands and is forecast to weaken further over the next 48 hours, according to the hurricane center. Marie, located nearly 400 miles off the coast of Mexico’s Baja California Peninsula, is strengthening. The storm could generate strong swells for portions of Mexico’s southwestern coast and Baja California through the weekend, and perhaps Southern California, too, according to the hurricane center. The trio of hurricanes represent a level of elevated activity consistent with El Niño, a natural climate pattern characterized by warmer-than-usual sea surface temperatures in parts of the Pacific Ocean. This year, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and other forecasting agencies predict an exceptionally strong El Niño, or “super El Niño,” marked by water temperatures at least 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above average in the Pacific. NOAA’s forecast last month suggested that this El Niño event has a 69% chance of becoming the strongest on record. El Niño typically exacerbates warming from human-caused climate change, further boosting global temperatures and increasing the likelihood of extreme weather. In El Niño years, the high sea surface temperatures help more Pacific storms to form and grow. Daniel Gilford, a meteorologist and atmospheric scientist at the nonprofit research group Climate Central, likened tropical cyclones to a car engine, with warm ocean water acting like fuel. “The engine needs some sort of fuel to convert into wind,” he said. “If we increase the amount of fuel available to a storm, it’s kind of like increasing the speed limit on your car. If we have extra fuel, we can push the accelerator down more and these storms can become more intense as a result.” This El Niño event has taken hold at a time when sea surface temperatures in the Pacific were already significantly elevated. Scientists have been tracking a vast marine heat wave — a prolonged period of unusually high ocean temperatures — in the Pacific that began last year. Gilford said that Climate Central’s early studies have found that about 94% of the Pacific has experienced heat wave conditions since January, with some regions already up to 2 degrees Celsius warmer than normal. “Temperatures across the entire Pacific Ocean are elevated, and we’re certainly seeing that in the region where these hurricanes and tropical cyclones are traversing,” he said. In contrast to the flurry of activity in the Pacific, things are relatively quiet in the Atlantic basin — yet another characteristic of El Niño, according to Gilford. “El Niño conditions change the winds in the atmosphere in such a way that they are not conducive to storms forming in the Atlantic Ocean,” he said. “That’s exactly what we’re seeing right now.” Although El Niño is a natural pattern, climate scientists think it may be intensifying as a result of climate change. A study in the journal Science last month found that El Niño events have strengthened since humans started burning fossil fuels that send heat-trapping greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said Thursday that El Niño is “being supersized before our eyes,” a situation that should be a call to action. “The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up,” Guterres said in response to a new World Meteorological Organization report on the strengthening El Niño. “Sea surface temperatures are rising, temperatures keep climbing, and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather. The race now is between rising risks and our commitment to take climate action and protect people. We must win that race.”

articles.title: In 1923, a Colorado businessman opened a hotel around an abandoned railway station beside giant petrified tree stumps; four decades later his 160-acre resort became part of a national monument
articles.summary: US News: In the spring of 1923, John D. Coplen opened a hotel on his ranch in Florissant, Colorado, built around the town's old railway station, which he had m.
articles.body: In the spring of 1923, John D. Coplen opened a hotel on his ranch in Florissant, Colorado, built around the town's old railway station, which he had moved onto the property and renovated into a lodge. The hotel stood near giant petrified redwood stumps and an outcropping of fossil shale, turning a site Coplen had spent decades protecting into a commercial attraction for visitors. Coplen was 75 by then and had built a successful career in mining and business across the American West. He had overseen the largely unoccupied Colorado ranch for almost 35 years, but his vision for the fossil beds had never changed. He believed that improving the site and adding a hotel would allow the public to experience its fossils in a way that resembled an early geological theme park. More than 2,900 people visited during the resort's first summer, with Coplen and his wife personally giving tours.How John Coplen's family connection led him to Florissant's fossil bedsCoplen's connection to the Florissant fossil beds began through his sister, naturalist Charlotte Hill. Charlotte and her husband, Adam, had purchased land in the Florissant Valley in 1874 and established what they called the Petrified Stump Ranch. The property sat in the middle of one of the richest fossil sites then known, containing enormous petrified redwood stumps and fossil-rich shale. Charlotte and Adam operated the ranch as a tourist and scientific site, giving visitors access to the fossils while also working with scientists interested in the discoveries. Coplen was already familiar with the site through his sister's work. In 1883, a group of Denver businessmen formed the Colorado Museum Association to buy the ranch and protect its fossils from being collected and shipped to museums and universities in the East. Coplen led the association. At the time, Colorado had few public resources available for preserving its scientific collections, so the group hoped to create a state museum and keep the fossil beds accessible within Colorado.Why the Colorado Museum Association's conservation plan fell apartFor the next 20 years, the association owned and operated the ranch almost like a private conservatory. Visitors and scientists could enter only with special permission, limiting the uncontrolled collecting that had already threatened the fossil beds. But the association's plan for a state museum never materialised, and the organisation dissolved in 1903. By then, Coplen had become a very wealthy businessman with mining interests in Arizona, New Mexico and Colorado. He bought out the remaining investors and took full ownership of the ranch, including its petrified wood and fossil specimens. The property was eventually renamed the Coplen Petrified Forest Hotel and Resort of Florissant. Coplen's decision was influenced by more than conservation. He believed the fossil beds could also become a public attraction. After years of leaving the ranch largely unoccupied, he returned to Florissant with his wife and sister each summer from 1922 to 1924 to oversee construction of the hotel. The old Florissant railway station was moved to the ranch and renovated into the lodge, which was positioned near the petrified stumps and fossil shale. A road was also laid out to the hotel before it opened in spring 1923.How a career in copper mining helped fund Coplen's fossil bed resortCoplen had built his fortune through mining and business. Born in Indiana in 1844, he moved with his family to the pioneer settlement of Colorado City when he was 16 and later established himself in Colorado's mining industry. In 1904, he moved to Globe, Arizona, to oversee the Inspiration Copper Mine Company. A self-trained mining engineer, Coplen developed a less expensive method for extracting copper from low-grade ore, helping the Inspiration Mine become one of the largest copper producers in the United States. By the time he retired to a large ranch near Riverside, California, Coplen still had mining interests, a large dairy farm in New Mexico and the fossil property in Colorado. At 75, he returned to Florissant with his wife and sister to supervise the hotel project. Once it opened, he and his wife gave tours themselves. More than 2,900 visitors came during the first summer, showing that Coplen's idea of turning the fossil beds into a destination could work.How Coplen's 160-acre resort eventually became part of a national monumentCoplen sold the 160-acre resort in 1927, a year before his death. The property continued to operate as a private tourist attraction under later owners, eventually becoming part of the history of what is now Florissant Fossil Beds National Monument. Congress established the national monument in 1969, and the National Park Service later acquired the former Coplen property in 1973. Today, more than 80,000 people visit Florissant Fossil Beds National Monument each year. The site protects the giant petrified redwood stumps and fossil-rich layers that first attracted scientists and tourists in the 19th century, including the same fossil landscape Coplen had spent decades trying to preserve and turn into a public attraction. The old railway station that became his lodge is also part of the site's history, a reminder that long before Florissant became a national monument, it was already being developed as a place where visitors could come to see the fossil record for themselves.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Nigel Farage says his aides' donor comments were 'loose pub talk'
articles.summary: Two senior Reform aides have stepped down from their roles following a Channel 4 News and Verbatim film about donations.
articles.body:
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has described secretly-recorded comments by his senior aides about donations as "injudicious" and "loose pub talk".

James Orr, the party's head of policy, and Dan Jukes, a close aide to Farage, have both stepped down and Reform has launched an internal investigation into the allegations.

It comes after Channel 4 News broadcast undercover filming by Verbatim Investigations, in which the two men suggested a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations for the party, one of which would have totalled £500,000.

Farage said his party had "done nothing wrong" and had taken "no illegal money. In fact no money was taken at all."

Electoral law sets out that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

In the Channel 4 report, which aired on Thursday night, a reporter posing as a potential party donor raises a concern to Farage's aide Dan Jukes that his American father wouldn't be able to directly give money to the party within the law.

Jukes tells him: "You do realise that you can do it?"

Channel 4 say Jukes was suggesting that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.

He then claims they have done it several times before, in exchanges bleeped out but which appear to refer to other instances where this mechanism had been used before.

At the press conference, Farage said that Channel 4 had opted to bleep the names, rather than broadcast them was because Jukes' claims were "simply not true".

He said those donations "haven't occurred" and "don't exist in our accounts".

Farage said his party took compliance around donations "very seriously".

Responding to the allegations, Jukes said: "This was entrapment over a prolonged period of nearly a year by foreign-funded climate change activists.

"I totally deny any wrongdoing but have stepped back from politics in order to clear my name."

Before stepping down from his position Jukes had been seen as Farage's right hand man.

Reform's head of policy, James Orr, who also appeared in the film, suggested to the undercover reporter that perhaps his American father could pay for opinion polling to aid Reform's campaigning.

In all, Channel 4 News claims three polls were commissioned in this way costing £32,500 in total and that the public was not told who commissioned or funded them.

Not disclosing such funding would be illegal and accepting this kind of foreign funding would also be illegal.

Orr told Sky News: "I have agreed to step down from my current role at Reform UK pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation into the conduct of the programme, with which I will cooperate fully."

In response to allegations of "entrapment" from Jukes, a spokesperson for Verbatim Investigations told BBC News the investigation was carried out "to the highest journalistic standards", adding: "As the footage shows, the plots we exposed were proposed by Mr Jukes and Mr Orr, not by our journalists."

Farage acknowledged Jukes' comments were "problematic" but added that they were "loose pub talk, including a couple of boasts that simply were not true".

"And whilst I'm aware that our people were pushed and pushed and pushed into saying these things, the comments were injudicious at best.

"Neither of these members were authorised to act in that way.

"Accordingly, they've stepped down pending an investigation, and I emphasise again: Reform has broken no law, and we take compliance around donations very, very seriously."

During the film, Farage is introduced to the undercover reporter posing as a party donor and an actor posing as his American father.

In the press conference, Farage said he was "annoyed" that he was introduced to the two men adding: "It should not have happened."

He said his party needed to "do better as we professionalise".

Labour and the Liberal Democrats have reported the party to the Metropolitan Police.

The police said it would assess the matter and any information provided to it.

In a statement on Friday, the Electoral Commission said: "We are considering all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit, and we are in touch with the Met Police."

A Channel 4 News spokesperson said: "We stand by the public interest journalism in this investigation, which has been rigorously verified to ensure accuracy.

"We would encourage people to watch the investigation in full."

articles.title: ‘Winds of change’: How Milei is stirring Falklands claim amid Trump-UK spat
articles.summary: Analysts say Argentina’s president sees an opportunity to exploit Trump’s growing tensions with London.
articles.body:
Argentina’s President Javier Milei is capitalising on his country’s long-running claim to the Falkland Islands by coupling threats of sanctions over a major offshore oil project with lavish praise for Donald Trump , after the US president publicly questioned Washington’s position over the disputed UK territory.

Milei’s remarks come as relations between Trump and the UK government have deteriorated over the UK’s refusal to support US military action against Iran, and as the right-wing Milei increasingly positions Argentina as one of Washington’s closest ideological allies in Latin America.

The UK has administered the Falkland Islands, which Argentina calls Las Malvinas, since 1833. However, as the islands lie off its shores, Argentina claims sovereignty over them.

The US has traditionally supported the UK’s claim to the territory. But analysts say Trump’s willingness to question established US policy, even if mainly intended as leverage against London, could provide Milei with an opportunity to unite Argentinians around one of the country’s few enduring national causes.

The question of Argentina’s claim to the islands was raised again this week when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s son, Yair, accused the UK of hypocrisy and wrote on X in Spanish: “The Falkland Islands belong to Argentina.”

What is the dispute over the Falkland Islands?

The Falklands are a self-governing British overseas territory in the South Atlantic, almost 13,000km (8,000 miles) from the UK.

Argentina says it inherited sovereignty over the islands from Spain in the 19th century. But Britain has administered the Falklands since 1833 and points both to that long presence and to the wishes of the islanders living there to justify its control. In a 2013 referendum, 1,513 of 1,517 voters backed remaining a British overseas territory.

The dispute erupted into war in 1982 when Argentina seized the islands.

The UK, under then-Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, sent a military force to retake the territory, with 74 days of fighting left 649 Argentine and 255 British service members dead.

In a nationally televised speech on Thursday, Milei seized on Trump’s suggestion that Washington might reconsider its position on the islands, and heralded the “winds of change” he said were blowing in favour of Argentina’s claim to the Falkland Islands.

“The United States is considering this change in position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with Western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come,” Milei said.

He also announced measures aimed at obstructing development of the Sea Lion oil project, about 220km (140 miles) north of the islands. The Sea Lion field sits in waters administered by the Falklands, and Argentina considers the project an illegal exploitation of resources in waters it claims as its own.

Rockhopper Exploration, a UK-based oil and gas exploration and production company with interests in the Falkland Islands, and Israel’s Navitas Petroleum are set to begin drilling in the coming months, with oil production expected to begin in 2028.

Milei also threatened tougher sanctions against companies involved in the project and announced new funding for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego, Argentina’s southernmost province, to strengthen the country’s military presence near the islands.

“Argentina will not stand idly by,” he said. “Any further advance on the Malvinas Islands will be considered a violation of our national security.”

“We can argue about my style. We can disagree over fiscal or exchange-rate policy,” Milei added. “But there are causes that rise above any political difference. The Malvinas is one of them.”

Trump has stopped short of outright endorsing Argentina’s claim to the islands, but he has repeatedly raised the possibility that Washington’s position on the islands could change.

In an interview with the right-wing GB News in the UK this week, Trump appeared to suggest he might not come to the UK’s aid if a conflict erupts with Argentina over the Falkland Islands.

He said the UK “was not there to help me” with the war with Iran.

“We didn’t need help, but I did ask NATO, and I asked your former leader, ‘Why didn’t you send a couple of ships?'”

Asked separately by the BBC if the longstanding US position on the UK’s claim to the Falklands was under review, Trump said: “I always review every position. That’s just one of many.”

Trump’s comments followed reports that US defence officials were considering using Washington’s position on the Falklands as leverage to pressure the UK to increase military spending, including the possibility of opposing UK sovereignty over the islands.

The idea has been around for some time. In April, a leaked Pentagon email proposed reviewing US support for the UK’s position on the Falklands as a way to pressure London over its refusal to support US military action against Iran.

Christoph Bluth, a professor at the University of Bradford in the UK, told Al Jazeera that the context is crucial.

“Trump has not endorsed Argentina’s sovereignty claim; he has merely said the US position is under review,” Bluth said.

He added that the idea appeared to have originated “inside the Pentagon as leverage against Britain over defence spending and its refusal to support US action against Iran, not from a reassessment of the Falklands dispute itself”.

The UK has reiterated its position. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the UK’s commitment to the islands was “unshakeable”, while a spokesperson for Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the islanders had a right to determine their own future and that the UK’s commitment was “unwavering”.

Matthew Benwell, a specialist on the Falklands and geopolitics, told Al Jazeera that Trump’s comments would cause unease in both London and Stanley, the Falklands capital, but cautioned against viewing them as a policy change.

“At this stage, these are just remarks from President Trump,” he said. Whether they lead to a change in the US sovereignty position or an explicit call for negotiations “remains to be seen”, he said, adding that such a shift looked unlikely for now.

How can Milei make this situation work in his favour?

Washington has historically recognised the UK’s de facto administration of the islands without formally taking a position on sovereignty.

That neutrality has mattered to London. Klaus Dodds, a professor at Royal Holloway, University of London, told Al Jazeera that the UK has traditionally been able to rely on having a closer relationship with Washington than Argentina does.

“Now that has changed,” he said. With Trump still in office and closely aligned with Milei, Dodds said the Argentinian president is likely to view the moment as an opportunity “to take advantage whenever and wherever he can”.

Milei has appeared repeatedly at pro-Trump events in the US, attended his second inauguration and been called Trump’s “favourite president”.

Last year, Trump authorised a $20bn financial lifeline package for Argentina, tying support to Milei’s party succeeding in legislative elections. After his La Libertad Avanza party won, Trump authorised additional imports of Argentinian beef to the US.

Eleonora Natale, an analyst focusing on Latin American politics, said any US openness towards Argentina on the Falklands had to be seen within that wider relationship.

“Milei has become one of Trump’s closest ideological allies in Latin America,” she told Al Jazeera, pointing to shared positions on security, migration and scepticism towards multilateral institutions.

Tilmann Altenberg, a reader in Hispanic Studies at Cardiff University, also cautioned against interpreting Trump’s remarks as a settled shift over sovereignty.

His comments, Altenberg said, were “first and foremost a reflection on the relationship between the US and the UK, rather than a deliberate shift in US policy” towards the islands.

But he said Milei may nevertheless see the current alignment as “a window of opportunity” to advance Argentina’s position and strengthen his hand ahead of the 2027 election.

Could US support actually affect the dispute?

Analysts said a genuine change in Washington’s position would be significant, but its practical effects would be limited.

Dodds said abandoning neutrality would mark a break with a “fundamental tenet of US policy post-1982” and could be read as Trump rewarding Milei while punishing the UK for refusing to support US operations against Iran.

Bluth said US backing could give Argentina greater international leverage and make companies more cautious about investing in oil projects around the Falklands.

But, he added, it “would not be a material change or oblige Britain to negotiate sovereignty”.

Buenos Aires cannot physically prevent production at the Sea Lion oil field, Bluth added, but it can use sanctions and legal pressure against companies involved in developing it.

Trump’s remarks may also have symbolic value in Argentina even before any formal US decision, Altenberg added. In Buenos Aires they “might be perceived as a sign that the sovereignty question could be tabled before the international community again soon”, he said.
